```{r setup}
#| include: false
suppressPackageStartupMessages({

# Categorical palette, fixed order (validated: CVD-safe, labels required).
pal <- c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#eda100", "#e87ba4")

model_labels <- c(

model_cols <- setNames(pal, names(model_labels)[1:5])   # section 5 charts the original five

var_labels <- c(
  pass_off_diff = "Pass offense rating",

  pass_def_diff = "Pass defense rating",
  rush_def_diff = "Rush defense rating",
  home = "Home field",
  rest_diff = "Rest-day difference",
  home_off_bye = "Home team off bye",
  away_off_bye = "Away team off bye",
  home_short_week = "Home team short week",
  away_short_week = "Away team short week",
  away_travel_miles = "Away travel miles",
  tz_crossed = "Time zones crossed",
  div_game = "Divisional game",

  home_qb_backup = "Home QB is backup",
  away_qb_backup = "Away QB is backup",
  qb_adj_diff = "QB rating gap (starter vs. team mix)",
  dome = "Dome / closed roof",
  temp = "Temperature",
  wind = "Wind",
  turf = "Artificial turf",
  spread = "Closing spread",
  strength = "Team strength (4 ratings)",
  situational = "Situational (10 variables)",
  qb = "QB (status flags; + rating gap in QB models)",
  environment = "Environment (4 variables)"
)
lab <- function(x) unname(ifelse(x %in% names(var_labels), var_labels[x], x))

theme_report <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      text = element_text(colour = ink),
      axis.text = element_text(colour = ink2),
      axis.title = element_text(colour = ink2, size = 10),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = grid_col, linewidth = 0.4),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),

      legend.title = element_blank(),
      legend.text = element_text(colour = ink2)
    )
}

kable <- function(df, digits = 3) knitr::kable(df, digits = digits, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
partial_label <- function(s) ifelse(s == 2026, "2026 (partial)", as.character(s))
# "+0.123 [-0.050, +0.290]": a bootstrap estimate with its 95% interval.
fmt_ci <- function(est, lo, hi, digits) {
  f <- paste0("%+.", digits, "f")
  sprintf(paste0(f, " [", f, ", ", f, "]"), est, lo, hi)
}
```

## 1. Question and data

The question: which pre-game variables best predict NFL game outcomes, and why?
Outcomes are modeled two ways: **point margin** (home score minus away score) with
linear regression, and **win/loss** with logistic regression (ties count as half a
win). Every variable is known before kickoff.

Data come from nflverse via `nflreadr`: play-by-play for team ratings and schedules
for game-level variables. The 2009 season is loaded only so 2010's week 1 ratings
have a prior season to carry over from. The 2026 season is included through the
games completed when the pipeline last ran.

```{r data-table}
res$n_games |>
  mutate(season = partial_label(season)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = season, values_from = games) |>
  kable()
```

Games dropped for missing features: **`r res$dropped`**. Games whose outdoor weather
was not recorded (mostly retractable roofs left open) get the stadium's median
temperature and wind for that season, then its median across all seasons.

<!-- NOAH: your interpretation here -->

## 2. How team strength is calculated

Each week, before that week's games, one weighted ridge regression is fit on every
run and pass play from the current and previous season:

> play EPA = offense strength + defense strength + home-field

That gives each team four ratings: pass offense, rush offense, pass defense, and
rush defense. Defense is signed so higher is better. Because every play involves
both an offense and a defense, each rating is already adjusted for the opponent.
Plays are down-weighted by age (a half-life in weeks); last season's plays get extra
decay for the offseason, which produces the preseason carryover. Plays in garbage
time (win probability below 5% or above 95%) count at a quarter weight.

The half-life, offseason decay, and ridge penalty were chosen using 2010–2017 only,
by how well each week's ratings explained that week's margins:

```{r tuning}
best <- res$tuning$best
tibble(
  Setting = c("Half-life (weeks)", "Offseason decay (weeks)", "Ridge penalty (lambda)",
              "Garbage-time weight"),
  Value = c(best$half_life, best$offseason_weeks, best$lambda, best$garbage_weight)
) |> kable(digits = 4)
```

The baseline uses each team's plain mean EPA/play over its last 8 games, with no
opponent adjustment. Both rating methods feed the same full model:

```{r ridge-vs-rolling}
res$scores |>
  filter(model %in% c("full_ridge", "full_rolling")) |>
  group_by(Model = model_labels[model]) |>
  summarise(`Margin RMSE` = mean(rmse), `Log loss` = mean(log_loss),
            `Win accuracy` = mean(accuracy), `Seasons` = n()) |>
  kable()
```

The latest ratings, for the next week to be played
(**`r max(res$ratings_ridge$season)` week
`r max(res$ratings_ridge$week[res$ratings_ridge$season == max(res$ratings_ridge$season)])`**):

```{r latest-ratings}
latest <- res$ratings_ridge |>
  filter(season == max(season)) |>
  filter(week == max(week))
latest |>
  mutate(Overall = pass_off + rush_off + pass_def + rush_def) |>
  arrange(desc(Overall)) |>
  transmute(Team = team, `Pass off` = pass_off, `Rush off` = rush_off,
            `Pass def` = pass_def, `Rush def` = rush_def, Overall) |>
  kable()
```

## 3. QB ratings

Team pass ratings blend every QB who played for a team. This section rates QBs
individually, so a backup start shows up as a weaker passing game.

Each week, before that week's games, one weighted ridge regression is fit on every
dropback (pass, sack or scramble) from the current and previous four seasons:

> dropback EPA = QB strength + defense strength + home-field + experience level

A QB's experience level is his career dropbacks before the game (0–99, 100–499,
500–1499, 1500+, counted from 2006). QB strengths are shrunk toward zero, so a QB
with few dropbacks is rated close to the typical QB at his experience level, which
for 0–99 dropbacks is well below average. Ratings follow the QB, not the team.

The **starter adjustment** compares the starter with the QBs whose plays built the
team's pass rating: starter rating minus the average rating of those QBs, weighted the
same way the team rating weights their plays. When the usual starter plays it is about
zero. The model uses the home-minus-away difference, the **QB rating gap**.

A simpler benchmark rates each QB by his plain mean EPA over his last 300 dropbacks
(padded with the average of low-experience QBs when he has fewer), with the same
starter adjustment.

QB half-life and ridge penalty were chosen on 2010–2017: among settings within 0.02
RMSE of the best on all games, the one best on games where a starter changed or a
backup started.

```{r qb-tuning}
qb_best <- res$qb_tuning$best
res$qb_tuning$scores |>
  arrange(rmse) |>
  transmute(`Half-life (weeks)` = qb_half_life, `Ridge penalty` = qb_lambda,
            `RMSE, all games` = rmse, `RMSE, QB-change games` = rmse_qb_change,
            Chosen = ifelse(qb_half_life == qb_best$qb_half_life & qb_lambda == qb_best$qb_lambda,
                            "✓", "")) |>
  kable(digits = 4)
```

```{r qb-latest}
qb_season <- max(res$qb_ratings_ridge$season)
qb_week <- max(res$qb_ratings_ridge$week[res$qb_ratings_ridge$season == qb_season])
starters_now <- res$qb_starters |>
  filter(season == qb_season) |>
  arrange(week) |>
  group_by(qb_id) |>
  summarise(team = last(team), .groups = "drop")
qb_table <- res$qb_ratings_ridge |>
  filter(season == qb_season, week == qb_week) |>
  inner_join(starters_now, by = "qb_id") |>
  left_join(res$qb_names, by = "qb_id") |>
  arrange(desc(qb_rating)) |>
  transmute(QB = coalesce(qb_name, qb_id), Team = team, `Rating (EPA/dropback)` = qb_rating,
            `Career dropbacks` = career_dropbacks)
f_qb <- res$features_ridge
backup_adj <- c(f_qb$home_qb_adj[f_qb$home_qb_backup == 1], f_qb$away_qb_adj[f_qb$away_qb_backup == 1])
```

Ratings for **`r qb_season` week `r qb_week`**, among QBs who have started, or are
projected to start, a game this season. Rating 0 = the average dropback.

```{r qb-top-bottom}
head(qb_table, 10) |> kable()
tail(qb_table, 10) |> kable()
```

Sanity check: in **`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(backup_adj < 0))`** of
`r length(backup_adj)` backup starts (2010 onward), the backup's adjustment is
negative. Dropbacks without a player ID left out: `r res$excluded_dropbacks`. Games
with a missing starter ID (adjustment set to 0): `r res$missing_starters`.

### Accuracy with QB ratings

RMSE by test season, on all games and on games where either team's starter changed
or a backup started (2026 is partial):

```{r qb-accuracy}
qb_models <- c("full_ridge", "full_qb_ridge", "full_qb_rolling", "spread_only")
qb_season_table <- function(df) {
  df |>
    filter(model %in% qb_models) |>
    transmute(Season = partial_label(season), model = model_labels[model], rmse) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = rmse) |>
    kable()
}
qb_season_table(res$scores)
qb_season_table(filter(res$scores_qb_subset, subset == "qb_change"))
bind_rows(mutate(res$scores, subset = "All games"),
          mutate(filter(res$scores_qb_subset, subset == "qb_change"), subset = "QB-change games")) |>
  filter(model %in% qb_models, season <= 2025) |>
  group_by(Games = subset, Model = model_labels[model]) |>
  summarise(`Margin RMSE` = mean(rmse), `Log loss` = mean(log_loss),
            `Games per season` = mean(n_games), .groups = "drop") |>
  kable()
```

### Do QB ratings earn their place?

The rule was fixed before any results. Seasons 2018–2025 count; 2026 does not. QB
ratings earn their place if either:

- **Path 1 (all games):** the QB model beats the full model on both RMSE and log loss
  (95% interval of the difference entirely below 0), and has lower RMSE in at least 5
  of the 8 seasons; or
- **Path 2 (QB-change games):** on QB-change games, the QB model beats the full model
  on RMSE (interval entirely below 0), and on all games its RMSE and log loss are no
  worse.

```{r qb-verdict}
v <- res$qb_verdict
bind_rows(mutate(res$qb_all_comparison, Games = "All games"),
          mutate(res$qb_subset_comparison, Games = "QB-change games")) |>
  transmute(Subset = Games,
            `Δ RMSE [95% interval]` = fmt_ci(d_rmse, d_rmse_low, d_rmse_high, 3),
            `Δ log loss [95% interval]` = fmt_ci(d_log_loss, d_log_loss_low, d_log_loss_high, 4),
            `Games scored` = n_games) |>
  kable()
```

Δ is the QB model (ridge) minus the full model, 2018–2025; negative means the QB model
is better. Seasons with lower RMSE: **`r v$seasons_better` of `r v$n_seasons`**.
Path 1: **`r ifelse(v$path1_all_games, "passed", "not passed")`**. Path 2:
**`r ifelse(v$path2_qb_change, "passed", "not passed")`**. Verdict: QB ratings
**`r ifelse(v$earns_place, "earn", "do not earn")`** their place.

Other comparisons (all test seasons, 2026 included):

```{r qb-comparisons}
res$model_comparisons |>
  filter(model_b %in% c("full_qb_ridge", "full_qb_rolling", "market_qb")) |>
  transmute(Model = model_labels[model_b], `Compared with` = model_labels[model_a],
            `Δ RMSE [95% interval]` = fmt_ci(d_rmse, d_rmse_low, d_rmse_high, 3),
            `Δ log loss [95% interval]` = fmt_ci(d_log_loss, d_log_loss_low, d_log_loss_high, 4)) |>
  kable()
```

```{r qb-coef}
res$coefs_qb |>
  filter(term == "qb_adj_diff") |>
  transmute(Model = model, Estimate = estimate, `95% low` = conf_low, `95% high` = conf_high) |>
  kable()
```

The QB rating gap coefficient is per 1 SD of the gap (2010–2025 fit): points of
margin in the margin model, log-odds in the win model. Ablation for the QB models is
in sections 7 and 8.

## 4. Effect sizes

Coefficients from the margin model fit on 2010–2025. Numeric variables are
standardized, so each bar reads as **points of margin per 1 standard deviation**.
Binary flags (yes/no) read as points when the flag is on. Lines show 95% confidence
intervals; a line crossing zero means the effect isn't distinguishable from noise.

The two kinds of variable are on different scales, so each gets its own panel.

```{r coefficients, fig.height=7.5}
cf <- res$coefs |>
  filter(model == "margin", term != "(Intercept)") |>
  mutate(label = lab(term),
         kind = factor(ifelse(term %in% BINARY_FEATURES, "Yes/no flags: points when on",
                              "Numeric: points per 1 SD"),
                       levels = c("Numeric: points per 1 SD", "Yes/no flags: points when on")),
         label = reorder(label, estimate))
ggplot(cf, aes(x = estimate, y = label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = ink2, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = conf_low, xmax = conf_high), colour = pal[1], linewidth = 2) +
  geom_point(colour = pal[1], size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~kind, ncol = 1, scales = "free") +
  labs(title = "Margin model coefficients",
       subtitle = "Points of home margin; 95% confidence intervals",
       x = "Points", y = NULL) +
  theme_report() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0, colour = ink))
```

```{r home-edge}
#| include: false
# Predicted home margin for evenly matched teams at a true home game, with every
# other variable at its 2010-2025 average. Numeric variables are standardized, so
# "average" is 0; binary flags take their average share; strength diffs are 0.
b <- res$coefs |> filter(model == "margin")
coef_of <- function(t) b$estimate[b$term == t]
train <- res$features_ridge |> filter(season <= 2025)
flags <- setdiff(intersect(BINARY_FEATURES, b$term), "home")
z_strength <- sapply(FEATURE_GROUPS$strength, function(v) (0 - mean(train[[v]])) / sd(train[[v]]))
home_edge <- coef_of("(Intercept)") + coef_of("home") +
  sum(sapply(flags, function(v) coef_of(v) * mean(train[[v]]))) +
  sum(sapply(FEATURE_GROUPS$strength, function(v) coef_of(v) * z_strength[[v]]))
raw_home <- mean(train$margin[train$home == 1])
```

**Home-field advantage:** almost every game is a true home game, so the "Home field"
coefficient only measures the difference between a true home game and a neutral
site, which is why its interval is wide. The useful number is the model's
prediction for two evenly matched teams at a true home game, with every other
variable at its average: **the home team by `r sprintf("%.1f", home_edge)` points**.
For comparison, the raw average home margin in 2010–2025 was
`r sprintf("%.1f", raw_home)` points.

The two short-week flags have very wide intervals because they almost always occur
together: on Thursday games both teams are usually on short rest, so the model can't
tell the two apart.

```{r coefficients-table}
cf |>
  arrange(desc(abs(estimate))) |>
  transmute(Variable = as.character(label), Estimate = estimate,
            `95% low` = conf_low, `95% high` = conf_high) |>
  kable()
```

## 5. Walk-forward accuracy

For each test season, every model is trained only on earlier seasons (starting in
2010) and then predicts that season. Lower is better for both metrics. The closing
spread is the market's prediction and the real benchmark to beat.

```{r accuracy, fig.height=5}
sc <- res$scores |>
  filter(model %in% names(model_cols)) |>
  mutate(Model = factor(model_labels[model], levels = model_labels[names(model_cols)]))
end_labels <- sc |> group_by(Model) |> filter(season == max(season))

accuracy_plot <- function(metric, title, ylab) {
  ggplot(sc, aes(season, .data[[metric]], colour = Model)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
    geom_point(size = 2.5) +
    ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = end_labels, aes(label = Model), size = 3, colour = ink2,
                             direction = "y", hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.25, segment.colour = grid_col,
                             min.segment.length = 0, box.padding = 0.15, show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(model_cols, model_labels[names(model_cols)])) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = unique(sc$season), labels = partial_label(unique(sc$season)),
                       expand = expansion(mult = c(0.03, 0.4))) +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = ylab) +
    theme_report() +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
}
accuracy_plot("rmse", "Margin error by test season", "RMSE (points)")
accuracy_plot("log_loss", "Win-probability error by test season", "Log loss")
```

```{r accuracy-table}
sc |>
  group_by(Model) |>
  summarise(`Margin RMSE` = mean(rmse), MAE = mean(mae), `Log loss` = mean(log_loss),
            Brier = mean(brier), `Win accuracy` = mean(accuracy)) |>
  kable()
```

Averages above are across test seasons 2018–2026; 2026 is a partial season.

### Is the gap bigger than noise?

Each row compares a model with a reference model on the same games. A paired
bootstrap redraws the test set 2,000 times by resampling whole weeks (all games in a
season-week together, since they share rating updates, weather and news), and
rescores both models on each redraw. Positive Δ means the model is worse than the one
it's compared with. The interval is the middle 95% of the redraws, and "share worse"
is the fraction of redraws in which the model lost. Δ is measured over all test games
pooled, so it can differ slightly from the gap between the season averages above.

```{r model-comparisons}
res$model_comparisons |>
  transmute(Model = model_labels[model_b], `Compared with` = model_labels[model_a],
            `Δ RMSE [95% interval]` = fmt_ci(d_rmse, d_rmse_low, d_rmse_high, 3),
            `Share worse (RMSE)` = share_worse_rmse,
            `Δ log loss [95% interval]` = fmt_ci(d_log_loss, d_log_loss_low, d_log_loss_high, 4),
            `Share worse (log loss)` = share_worse_log_loss) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

## 6. Calibration

When the full model (ridge ratings) says a team wins 70% of the time, does it? Each
point is a bin of predictions from every test season; points on the dashed line
mean the probabilities can be taken at face value. Point size shows how many games
are in the bin.

```{r calibration, fig.height=5, fig.width=5.5}
ggplot(res$calibration, aes(mean_pred, actual_rate)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = ink2) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), colour = pal[1]) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 8, name = "Games") +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Calibration: full model, ridge ratings",
       x = "Predicted home win probability", y = "Actual home win rate") +
  theme_report() +
  theme(legend.position = "right", legend.title = element_text(colour = ink2, size = 9))
```

```{r calibration-table}
res$calibration |>
  transmute(Bin = bin, `Mean predicted` = mean_pred, `Actual win rate` = actual_rate, Games = n) |>
  kable()
```

## 7. What matters: ablation

Each bar shows how much worse the walk-forward margin error gets when a group (or a
single variable) is removed from the full model, measured over all test games pooled.
Bigger bars mean the variable carries more predictive value. Negative bars mean the
model did *better* without it. The whisker is a 95% interval from the same paired
week-block bootstrap as in section 5, and the label shows in how many seasons
removing it hurt.

**Reading the intervals.** Sections 7 and 8 test about 100 comparisons between them,
so even if none of these variables mattered, about five 95% intervals would exclude
0 by chance. Trust a bar whose interval clears 0 comfortably *and* that hurt in most
seasons; a bar that only just clears 0, or that hurt in only a few seasons, may be
noise.

```{r ablation-plot-fn}
# Pooled bootstrap estimates joined to the per-season "seasons hurt" counts.
ablation_summary <- function(abl, boot) {
  inner_join(boot, summarize_ablation(abl), by = "dropped") |>
    arrange(desc(d_rmse))
}
ablation_plot <- function(abl, boot, title) {
  s <- ablation_summary(abl, boot) |>
    mutate(label = reorder(lab(dropped), d_rmse),
           helps = ifelse(d_rmse > 0, "Removing it hurts", "Removing it helps"),
           seasons_txt = paste0(seasons_hurt, "/", n_seasons))
  ggplot(s, aes(d_rmse, label, fill = helps)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.7) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = ink2, linewidth = 0.4) +
    geom_linerange(aes(xmin = d_rmse_low, xmax = d_rmse_high), colour = ink, linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_text(aes(x = ifelse(d_rmse >= 0, d_rmse_high, d_rmse_low), label = seasons_txt,
                  hjust = ifelse(d_rmse >= 0, -0.2, 1.2)),
              size = 3, colour = ink2) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Removing it hurts" = pal[1], "Removing it helps" = pal[2]),
                      breaks = c("Removing it hurts", "Removing it helps")) +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.18)) +
    labs(title = title,
         subtitle = "Whisker = 95% week-block bootstrap interval; label = seasons where removing it hurt",
         x = "Increase in margin RMSE when removed (points, all test games)", y = NULL) +
    theme_report()
}
ablation_table <- function(abl, boot) {
  ablation_summary(abl, boot) |>
    transmute(Removed = lab(dropped),
              `Δ RMSE [95% interval]` = fmt_ci(d_rmse, d_rmse_low, d_rmse_high, 3),
              `Δ log loss [95% interval]` = fmt_ci(d_log_loss, d_log_loss_low, d_log_loss_high, 4),
              `Seasons hurt` = paste0(seasons_hurt, "/", n_seasons)) |>
    kable()
}
```

```{r ablation-qb, fig.height=7.5}
ablation_plot(res$ablation_qb_groups, res$ablation_qb_groups_boot, "Variable groups, QB model")

ablation_plot(res$ablation_qb_vars, res$ablation_qb_vars_boot, "Individual variables, QB model")
ablation_table(res$ablation_qb_vars, res$ablation_qb_vars_boot)
```

## 8. After the market

The same drop-one test, run on the model that already includes the closing spread.
This asks which variables still add predictive value once the market's opinion is
known, which is the question that matters for beating Kalshi and Polymarket prices.
The same caution as in section 7 applies: with about 100 intervals across the two
sections, expect about five to exclude 0 by chance, so trust bars whose interval clears
0 comfortably and that hurt in most seasons.

```{r ablation-market, fig.height=7.5}
ablation_plot(res$ablation_market_vars, res$ablation_market_vars_boot,
              "Variables, given the closing spread")
ablation_table(res$ablation_market_vars, res$ablation_market_vars_boot)
```

## 9. Caveats and next steps

**Caveats**

- **Starting QB is the actual starter.** The schedule records who started, which is
  usually known before kickoff, but a surprise game-day scratch leaks a little
  information the model wouldn't have had.
- **"Backup QB"** means the starter isn't the team's most common starter over its
  previous 8 games. A new starter counts as a backup for his first few games, even
  if the change was planned (for example, a rookie named the week 1 starter).
- **Scrambles count twice in one case.** Team rush ratings include QB scrambles, and
  QB ratings include them too. When the usual starter plays this cancels out (his
  adjustment is about zero). When a scrambling starter is replaced, the team's rush
  rating still carries his scrambles for a few weeks, so the backup's team looks a
  little better on the ground than it is.
- **Designed QB runs are not in QB ratings.** They stay in the team's rush rating, so
  replacing a running QB lowers the QB gap only for his passing, sacks and scrambles;
  the team's rush rating keeps his designed runs until it catches up.
- **QB history starts in 2006.** Career dropback counts for QBs who began before 2006
  are undercounted. About 90 of the roughly 8,900 starts from 2010 on (about 1%), by
  veterans such as Michael Vick, Rex Grossman, Kerry Collins and Charlie Batch, fall
  in a lower experience level than their real careers would put them in.
- **The upcoming week uses projected starters** from the schedule, which can change
  before kickoff.
- **Weather for open retractable roofs** is filled from stadium medians, not
  measured.
- **Home and away short-week flags overlap almost completely** (both teams are on
  short rest in nearly every Thursday game), so their individual coefficients are
  unreliable even though their combined effect is estimable.
- **Effects are linear with no interactions.** Curves and interactions are left for
  the next step, where they have to earn their place in walk-forward accuracy.
- **2026 is a partial season**, so its accuracy numbers are noisier.

**Next steps**

1. An xgboost check: if boosting beats this regression in walk-forward accuracy,
   SHAP values point to the nonlinearity or interaction the linear model misses.
2. Bring `R/team_strength.R` and `R/features.R` into the Forecast Lab, and compare
   win probabilities against Kalshi and Polymarket prices.
